COM747 Week 10: Data Analytics, Data Engineering and Black-Box Methods

Lecture demonstrations and complete seminar solutions

How to use this notebook. The guest lecture showed an investigative analyst’s process (load → validate → transform → present) on a fraud case. Part A rebuilds that process in R on made-up data, including real SQL run against an in-memory database, so you can see the R and SQL side by side. Part B completes seminar Exercise 1 (strengths and weaknesses of supervised methods) and Part C completes Exercise 2 (neural networks and SVMs, “black box” methods). No data files are needed.

library(DBI); library(RSQLite)     # SQL inside R
library(dplyr)                      # joins and summaries, tidyverse style
library(neuralnet)                  # install.packages("neuralnet")
library(e1071)                      # svm()
library(class); library(rpart)      # knn(), decision trees for comparison

Part A: The analyst’s process in R

A1. Simulate the client’s data

Three tables, as in the case: log books (scanned, with messy names), employee details, and diesel claims. One driver (Murphy) claims diesel on some days with no trip.

set.seed(2024)
drivers <- c("Byrne", "Doyle", "Kelly", "Murphy", "Nolan", "Walsh")
days <- seq(as.Date("2024-01-01"), as.Date("2024-03-31"), by = "day")
workdays <- days[!weekdays(days) %in% c("Saturday", "Sunday")]

log_books <- do.call(rbind, lapply(drivers, function(d) {
  worked <- sort(sample(workdays, 50))
  data.frame(scanned_name = d, date = worked, duration = round(runif(50, 6, 10.5), 1))
}))
# scanning makes names messy: random case and stray spaces
messy <- sample(nrow(log_books), 60)
log_books$scanned_name[messy] <- toupper(log_books$scanned_name[messy])
log_books$scanned_name[messy[1:20]] <- paste0(" ", log_books$scanned_name[messy[1:20]], " ")

# diesel claims: about 12 litres per hour driven, priced per litre
diesel_claims <- transform(log_books, driver = trimws(tools::toTitleCase(tolower(scanned_name))),
                           litres = round(duration * rnorm(nrow(log_books), 12, 0.8)))[, c("driver", "date", "litres")]
# Murphy's extra claims on weekends (no log book trip)
weekend <- days[weekdays(days) == "Saturday"]
extra <- data.frame(driver = "Murphy", date = sample(weekend, 10), litres = round(runif(10, 70, 110)))
diesel_claims <- rbind(diesel_claims, extra)
diesel_claims$amount <- round(diesel_claims$litres * 1.68, 2)     # € per litre

employees <- data.frame(driver = drivers, depot = c("Cork", "Cork", "Dublin", "Dublin", "Galway", "Galway"),
                        truck_age = c(3, 7, 2, 4, 6, 5))
head(log_books); head(diesel_claims); employees
##   scanned_name       date duration
## 1        Byrne 2024-01-01      6.9
## 2        Byrne 2024-01-02      8.8
## 3        Byrne 2024-01-03      8.0
## 4        Byrne 2024-01-04      7.4
## 5        Byrne 2024-01-08      9.2
## 6       BYRNE  2024-01-09      7.3
##   driver       date litres amount
## 1  Byrne 2024-01-01     83 139.44
## 2  Byrne 2024-01-02    103 173.04
## 3  Byrne 2024-01-03     96 161.28
## 4  Byrne 2024-01-04     85 142.80
## 5  Byrne 2024-01-08    106 178.08
## 6  Byrne 2024-01-09     83 139.44
##   driver  depot truck_age
## 1  Byrne   Cork         3
## 2  Doyle   Cork         7
## 3  Kelly Dublin         2
## 4 Murphy Dublin         4
## 5  Nolan Galway         6
## 6  Walsh Galway         5

A2. Load into a database

con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")      # a throwaway SQL database in memory
dbWriteTable(con, "log_books_table", transform(log_books, date = as.character(date)))
dbWriteTable(con, "diesel_claims_table", transform(diesel_claims, date = as.character(date)))
dbWriteTable(con, "employees", employees)
dbListTables(con)
## [1] "diesel_claims_table" "employees"           "log_books_table"

A3. Validate: data sent = data loaded

fingerprint <- function(df) {
  num <- df[sapply(df, is.numeric)]
  list(cols = ncol(df), rows = nrow(df),
       stats = sapply(num, function(x) c(min = min(x), max = max(x), sum = sum(x))))
}
sent   <- fingerprint(diesel_claims)
loaded <- fingerprint(dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT * FROM diesel_claims_table"))
c(sent = sent$cols, loaded = loaded$cols)
##   sent loaded 
##      4      4
c(sent = sent$rows, loaded = loaded$rows)
##   sent loaded 
##    310    310
all.equal(sent$stats, loaded$stats)
## [1] TRUE
# The same checks in SQL
dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT COUNT(*) AS n_rows, MIN(amount) AS min_amt, MAX(amount) AS max_amt, SUM(amount) AS sum_amt
                 FROM diesel_claims_table")
##   n_rows min_amt max_amt  sum_amt
## 1    310  105.84  233.52 51779.28

What a broken load looks like (the file lost its last 12 rows and amounts were stored as integers):

broken <- head(diesel_claims, -12)
broken$amount <- floor(broken$amount)
b <- fingerprint(broken)
c(sent = sent$rows, loaded = b$rows)
##   sent loaded 
##    310    298
round(sent$stats[, "amount"] - b$stats[, "amount"], 2)    # every amount check differs
##     min     max     sum 
##    0.84    0.52 1979.28

A4. Transform: cleanse the names

table(log_books$scanned_name)[1:8]            # " MURPHY ", "MURPHY", "Murphy" are one person
## 
##   BYRNE    DOYLE    KELLY   MURPHY    NOLAN    WALSH     BYRNE    Byrne 
##        2        2        2        5        4        5        8       40
log_books$cleansed_name <- trimws(tools::toTitleCase(tolower(log_books$scanned_name)))
table(log_books$cleansed_name)
## 
##  Byrne  Doyle  Kelly Murphy  Nolan  Walsh 
##     50     50     50     50     50     50
dbWriteTable(con, "log_books_table", transform(log_books, date = as.character(date)), overwrite = TRUE)

A5. Transform: join (SQL and R)

The lecture’s query:

joined_sql <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT lb.cleansed_name, lb.date, lb.duration, dc.litres, dc.amount
  FROM log_books_table lb
  JOIN diesel_claims_table dc ON lb.cleansed_name = dc.driver AND lb.date = dc.date")
nrow(joined_sql); head(joined_sql)
## [1] 300
##   cleansed_name       date duration litres amount
## 1         Byrne 2024-01-01      6.9     83 139.44
## 2         Byrne 2024-01-02      8.8    103 173.04
## 3         Byrne 2024-01-03      8.0     96 161.28
## 4         Byrne 2024-01-04      7.4     85 142.80
## 5         Byrne 2024-01-08      9.2    106 178.08
## 6         Byrne 2024-01-09      7.3     83 139.44

The same in base R and dplyr:

joined_base <- merge(log_books, diesel_claims,
                     by.x = c("cleansed_name", "date"), by.y = c("driver", "date"))   # inner join
joined_dplyr <- inner_join(log_books, diesel_claims, by = c(cleansed_name = "driver", "date"))
c(sql = nrow(joined_sql), base = nrow(joined_base), dplyr = nrow(joined_dplyr))
##   sql  base dplyr 
##   300   300   300

The inner join silently drops claims with no matching trip, which are exactly the ones we care about. An anti-join finds them:

no_trip_sql <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT dc.* FROM diesel_claims_table dc
  LEFT JOIN log_books_table lb ON lb.cleansed_name = dc.driver AND lb.date = dc.date
  WHERE lb.cleansed_name IS NULL")
no_trip <- anti_join(diesel_claims, log_books, by = c(driver = "cleansed_name", "date"))
nrow(no_trip_sql); nrow(no_trip)
## [1] 10
## [1] 10
table(no_trip$driver)
## 
## Murphy 
##     10
no_trip %>% mutate(day = weekdays(date)) %>% count(driver, day)
##   driver      day  n
## 1 Murphy Saturday 10

Ask: Which join type would you have used first, and what would you have missed? Inner joins are the default in SQL; always count what didn’t match.

A6. Present: aggregate and visualise

per_driver <- diesel_claims %>% group_by(driver) %>% summarise(litres = sum(litres), claims = n(), euro = sum(amount)) %>%
  left_join(log_books %>% group_by(cleansed_name) %>% summarise(hours = sum(duration)), by = c(driver = "cleansed_name")) %>%
  left_join(employees, by = "driver") %>%
  mutate(litres_per_hour = round(litres / hours, 1))
per_driver
## # A tibble: 6 x 8
##   driver litres claims   euro hours depot  truck_age litres_per_hour
##   <chr>   <dbl>  <int>  <dbl> <dbl> <chr>      <dbl>           <dbl>
## 1 Byrne    4867     50  8177.  406. Cork           3            12  
## 2 Doyle    4901     50  8234.  409. Cork           7            12  
## 3 Kelly    5160     50  8669.  428. Dublin         2            12  
## 4 Murphy   5996     60 10073.  419  Dublin         4            14.3
## 5 Nolan    5127     50  8613.  426. Galway         6            12  
## 6 Walsh    4770     50  8014.  403. Galway         5            11.8
fleet_rate <- with(subset(per_driver, driver != "Murphy"), sum(litres) / sum(hours))
plot(litres ~ hours, data = per_driver, pch = 19, cex = 1.6,
     col = ifelse(per_driver$driver == "Murphy", "#b3372f", "#2b5fa6"),
     xlab = "Hours driven (log books)", ylab = "Litres claimed", main = "Fuel claimed against driving logged")
abline(0, fleet_rate, lty = 2)
text(per_driver$hours, per_driver$litres, per_driver$driver, pos = 4, cex = 0.8)

Evidence, not proof. Murphy’s ratio is well above the fleet’s, and the anti-join shows the extra claims fall on Saturdays. Before presenting, check alternative explanations (an older truck? missing log-book scans?) and say what the data can and can’t show. Here truck_age is 4 for Murphy, so age doesn’t explain it.

dbDisconnect(con)

A7. The data engineer’s version: a repeatable pipeline

An engineer would wrap the same steps in functions so the pipeline can run every time a new file lands, and stop if a check fails.

extract   <- function(path) read.csv(path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
validate  <- function(df, expected_rows, expected_cols) {
  if (nrow(df) != expected_rows) stop("Row count ", nrow(df), " != ", expected_rows)
  if (ncol(df) != expected_cols) stop("Column count ", ncol(df), " != ", expected_cols)
  invisible(df)
}
transform_claims <- function(df) df %>% mutate(date = as.Date(date)) %>% group_by(driver) %>% summarise(litres = sum(litres))
load_to_db <- function(df, con, name) { dbWriteTable(con, name, df, overwrite = TRUE); invisible(TRUE) }

# simulate a delivery arriving in the landing zone
landing <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv"); write.csv(diesel_claims, landing, row.names = FALSE)
con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
extract(landing) |> validate(expected_rows = nrow(diesel_claims), expected_cols = 4) |>
  transform_claims() |> load_to_db(con, "claims_by_driver")
dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT * FROM claims_by_driver ORDER BY litres DESC")
##   driver litres
## 1 Murphy   5996
## 2  Kelly   5160
## 3  Nolan   5127
## 4  Doyle   4901
## 5  Byrne   4867
## 6  Walsh   4770
# a bad delivery is stopped at validation, so nothing downstream runs
try(extract(landing) |> head(-5) |> validate(expected_rows = nrow(diesel_claims), expected_cols = 4))
## Error in validate(head(extract(landing), -5), expected_rows = nrow(diesel_claims),  : 
##   Row count 305 != 310
dbDisconnect(con)

Part B: Exercise 1, strengths and weaknesses

Completed from Lantz, Machine Learning with R, with an example of when you would and would not use each method.

Method Strengths Weaknesses Use it for… Avoid it for…
Decision trees Easy to explain as a flowchart; handles numeric and categorical data and missing values; selects important features; fast Unstable (small data changes alter the tree); overfits unless pruned; axis-parallel splits; biased towards features with many levels Credit or triage decisions that must be explained Very noisy data (use a random forest instead)
k-nearest neighbour Simple; no training; no assumptions about the distribution Choice of k; needs scaling; slow predictions on large data; no model to interpret; sensitive to irrelevant features and missing data Small, low-dimensional data; similarity-based recommendations Millions of rows needing real-time predictions
Neural networks Model almost any non-linear pattern; excellent on images, signals, speech, text Black box; needs lots of data and compute; many hyperparameters; overfits; needs scaled inputs ECG classification from a million labelled recordings Small tabular data where reasons are required
Support vector machines Accurate; robust to noise; good with many features (text, genes) Black box; kernel and parameter tuning by trial and error; slow on huge data; no probabilities by default Text and gene-expression classification When explanation or calibrated probabilities are needed
Multiple regression Interpretable coefficients with p-values and confidence intervals; widely understood Assumes linearity and well-behaved residuals; sensitive to outliers; you must specify the form Estimating how a price depends on several factors Strongly non-linear or interacting relationships
Logistic regression Probabilities and odds ratios; fast; strong baseline for binary outcomes Linear in the log-odds; struggles with separation and heavy imbalance Predicting survival or default with an explanation Images, complex interactions
Naive Bayes Fast, simple; robust to noise and missing data; good with many features and little data Assumes independent, equally important features; probabilities poorly calibrated; numeric features need care Spam filtering and text classification When features are strongly dependent and probabilities matter

Discuss: Which of these are “white box” (you can read the reasoning) and which are “black box”? Trees, regression, logistic regression and Naive Bayes are white box; k-NN is transparent per prediction but has no model; neural networks and SVMs are black box.

Part C: Exercise 2, black-box methods

C1. The sheet’s network

set.seed(1)
IrisDF <- iris
IrisDF$Species <- factor(IrisDF$Species)
model <- neuralnet(Species ~ Petal.Length + Petal.Width + Sepal.Width + Sepal.Length,
                   IrisDF, linear.output = FALSE)
# linear.output = FALSE: apply the logistic activation to the outputs too (classification)
model$result.matrix[1:3, ]      # error, threshold reached, steps
##             error reached.threshold             steps 
##      25.012203025       0.009497745      88.000000000
plot(model, rep = "best")       # rep = "best" draws it inside the notebook rather than a new window

The default is one hidden neuron. How good is it, even on the data it was trained on?

p <- predict(model, IrisDF)           # one column of scores per species
head(round(p, 3))
##       [,1]  [,2]  [,3]
## [1,] 0.986 0.001 0.001
## [2,] 0.986 0.001 0.001
## [3,] 0.986 0.001 0.001
## [4,] 0.986 0.001 0.001
## [5,] 0.986 0.001 0.001
## [6,] 0.986 0.001 0.001
pred <- levels(IrisDF$Species)[max.col(p)]
table(predicted = pred, actual = IrisDF$Species)
##             actual
## predicted    setosa versicolor virginica
##   setosa         50          0         0
##   versicolor      0         25        24
##   virginica       0         25        26
mean(pred == IrisDF$Species)
## [1] 0.6733333

Only about 67% on its own training data. Setosa is perfect, but versicolor and virginica get almost identical output weights, so the network can’t tell them apart. With one hidden neuron every flower is reduced to a single number, and the unscaled inputs make training harder. “There is no testing here” too. The fixes are below.

C2. Scale, split and use more hidden neurons

sc <- IrisDF
sc[, 1:4] <- scale(sc[, 1:4])                 # neural networks need inputs on similar scales
set.seed(1)
idx   <- sample(nrow(sc), 105)                # 70% train, 30% test
train <- sc[idx, ]; test <- sc[-idx, ]

set.seed(1)
nn3 <- neuralnet(Species ~ ., data = train, hidden = 3, linear.output = FALSE)
pred3 <- levels(sc$Species)[max.col(predict(nn3, test))]
table(predicted = pred3, actual = test$Species)
##             actual
## predicted    setosa versicolor virginica
##   setosa         15          0         0
##   versicolor      0         17         2
##   virginica       0          0        11
mean(pred3 == test$Species)
## [1] 0.9555556
plot(nn3, rep = "best")

C3. How many hidden neurons?

acc_nn <- function(hidden, seed) {
  set.seed(seed); idx <- sample(150, 105)
  m <- neuralnet(Species ~ ., sc[idx, ], hidden = hidden, linear.output = FALSE, stepmax = 1e5)
  mean(levels(sc$Species)[max.col(predict(m, sc[-idx, ]))] == sc$Species[-idx])
}
res <- expand.grid(hidden = c(1, 2, 3, 5), seed = 1:10)
res$acc <- mapply(acc_nn, res$hidden, res$seed)
aggregate(acc ~ hidden, res, function(a) round(c(mean = mean(a), min = min(a), max = max(a)), 3))
##   hidden acc.mean acc.min acc.max
## 1      1    0.904   0.600   0.978
## 2      2    0.931   0.889   0.956
## 3      3    0.931   0.911   0.956
## 4      5    0.929   0.822   0.956
boxplot(acc ~ hidden, res, xlab = "hidden neurons", ylab = "test accuracy", col = "#cfdcf0",
        main = "10 random splits per network size")

One hidden neuron is unreliable; two or three are consistently good. More neurons don’t help on this small problem and take longer to train.

C4. Other parameters to explore (?neuralnet)

set.seed(1)
two_layer <- neuralnet(Species ~ ., train, hidden = c(4, 2), linear.output = FALSE)  # two hidden layers
set.seed(1)
tanh_net  <- neuralnet(Species ~ ., train, hidden = 3, act.fct = "tanh", linear.output = FALSE)
set.seed(1)
backprop  <- neuralnet(Species ~ ., train, hidden = 3, algorithm = "backprop", learningrate = 0.01,
                       linear.output = FALSE, stepmax = 1e5)
acc <- function(m) mean(levels(sc$Species)[max.col(predict(m, test))] == test$Species)
sapply(list(two_layer = two_layer, tanh = tanh_net, backprop = backprop), function(m)
  c(test_accuracy = acc(m), steps = m$result.matrix["steps", 1]))
##                 two_layer         tanh     backprop
## test_accuracy   0.9333333    0.9333333 9.555556e-01
## steps.steps   428.0000000 2428.0000000 1.800300e+04
  • hidden = c(4, 2): two hidden layers of 4 and 2 neurons.
  • act.fct = "tanh": a different activation function (range −1 to 1).
  • algorithm = "backprop" with a learningrate: classic gradient descent, usually far more steps than the default resilient backpropagation ("rprop+").

C5. Support vector machines

for (k in c("linear", "polynomial", "radial")) {
  m <- svm(Species ~ ., data = train, kernel = k)
  cat(sprintf("%-10s test accuracy %.3f, support vectors %d\n", k, mean(predict(m, test) == test$Species), m$tot.nSV))
}
## linear     test accuracy 1.000, support vectors 23
## polynomial test accuracy 0.844, support vectors 48
## radial     test accuracy 0.978, support vectors 44
tuned <- tune(svm, Species ~ ., data = train, ranges = list(cost = c(0.1, 1, 10), gamma = c(0.05, 0.25, 1)))
tuned$best.parameters
##   cost gamma
## 2    1  0.05
mean(predict(tuned$best.model, test) == test$Species)
## [1] 0.9555556

C6. Everything on the same split

data.frame(method = c("k-NN (k = 5)", "decision tree", "SVM (radial)", "neural net (3)"),
  test_accuracy = c(mean(knn(train[, 1:4], test[, 1:4], train$Species, k = 5) == test$Species),
                    mean(predict(rpart(Species ~ ., train), test, type = "class") == test$Species),
                    mean(predict(svm(Species ~ ., train), test) == test$Species),
                    mean(pred3 == test$Species)))
##           method test_accuracy
## 1   k-NN (k = 5)     0.9333333
## 2  decision tree     0.9111111
## 3   SVM (radial)     0.9777778
## 4 neural net (3)     0.9555556

Ask: On iris every method scores above 90%. So how do you choose? By the other columns of the table in Part B: interpretability, data size, training and prediction time, and what the people using the model need.

Summary

Task R
SQL in R con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:"), dbWriteTable(), dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT ...")
Validate ncol(), nrow(), sapply(df, range), sum(), stopifnot()
Joins merge(x, y, by.x, by.y, all.x / all.y / all), inner_join(), left_join(), anti_join()
Aggregate aggregate(), group_by() |> summarise()
Neural network neuralnet(y ~ ., data, hidden = 3, linear.output = FALSE), predict(), plot(m, rep = "best")
SVM svm(y ~ ., data, kernel = "radial"), tune(svm, ..., ranges = list(cost, gamma))
